analysis.one_liner: Stops hospitals from billing patients for out-of-network care without notice or consent.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 45 cosponsors, never received a hearing or a vote in either House committee and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require hospitals participating in Medicare to tell patients up front whether their care would be out-of-network and estimate the extra cost, and to get written consent at least 24 hours before billing above in-network rates. For emergency and same-day services, hospitals could not charge more than the in-network cost-sharing amount. Hospitals that broke these rules could only bill the patient the in-network amount.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with health insurance who get care at hospitals: people who schedule procedures at in-network hospitals but are billed by out-of-network doctors they did not choose, and people treated in emergencies at hospitals outside their network. Instead of surprise bills for hundreds or thousands of dollars, they would pay only what an in-network provider would have charged.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured patients facing surprise hospital bills

how_it_helps.text: Requires hospitals to give written notice of whether the hospital or any provider treating the patient is out-of-network, plus an estimate of charges above normal cost sharing.
Requires signed patient consent at least 24 hours before care before a hospital can bill above in-network rates for out-of-network services.
Bars hospitals from charging more than in-network cost sharing for same-day services, including emergency care, so patients cannot be billed for surprise charges when they had no chance to consent.
Enforces the rules by making them a condition of Medicare participation, so hospitals that refuse to comply cannot bill above the in-network amount and risk losing Medicare enrollment.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and the doctors billing at hospitals (anesthesiologists, radiologists, emergency physicians, labs) would lose the ability to bill patients above in-network rates for out-of-network care they did not disclose and get consented. The most aggressive out-of-network billers would lose revenue; hospitals would face new notice and paperwork duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals and out-of-network providers billing at them

drawbacks.text: The consent-and-notice requirement applies broadly, including for routine scheduled care; the 24-hour written-consent rule adds paperwork for hospitals and could delay some scheduled services.

The bill caps what the patient pays but does not resolve what the insurer or out-of-network provider is paid, so payment disputes between insurers and providers would continue and could feed network narrowness or provider-lobbying pressure later.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to patients is large and direct: surprise bills, often thousands of dollars for care at an in-network hospital, would largely end. The costs fall on hospitals and on the physicians most likely to send surprise bills, plus modest administrative burden. Honest supporters acknowledge the notice-and-consent machinery is clunky for scheduled care and that the bill leaves insurer-provider payment fights untouched; the emergency cap is the cleanest part.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees, then to their Health subcommittees, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on February 2, 2017, with 32 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee.
It was then referred to the Health Subcommittee of Energy and Commerce on February 3 and to the Ways and Means Health Subcommittee on February 14, 2017.
No further action was recorded: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and physicians who profit from out-of-network billing avoided new limits and paperwork for another two years; insurers also avoided change. Insured patients kept facing surprise bills, and the issue was not resolved in that Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals and out-of-network billers, not patients

for.name: Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Surprise Billing Act of 2017 and recruited cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee, which took no recorded action; the committee never marked up or voted on the bill.

against.name: Hospital and physician billing interests
against.role: Hospitals and out-of-network specialists who bill at hospitals (emergency physicians, anesthesiologists, radiologists)
against.what_they_did: Would lose revenue from surprise out-of-network billing; these interests have historically lobbied hard against surprise-billing limits and no committee action followed.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was nearly all Democratic (44 of 45 cosponsors) with one Republican; the bill never reached a vote, so no floor votes exist to measure the split.

industries.industry: Hospitals and out-of-network providers billing at hospitals (emergency physicians, anesthesiologists, radiologists, labs)
industries.note: They would lose the ability to bill patients above in-network rates for out-of-network care without notice and consent, and would face notice and paperwork duties. Surprise billing is a major revenue source for some of these specialties, so the loss is direct.

Insurers would face fewer out-of-network claims beyond network cost sharing, since the bill caps patient liability but does not set provider payment. Broadly aligned with patients on ending surprise bills, though payment disputes with providers would remain.
